speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. I need to evaluate the cause of your systemic hypertension. How old are you, and have you been diagnosed with high blood pressure before?

speaker: Patient
text: 5-year-old boy. The patient is presented by his mother for a well-child visit. The boy was born at 39 weeks gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery, is currently up to date on all vaccines, and is meeting all developmental milestones. His mother reports that he has been generally doing well with no concerns. No family history of cardiovascular disease. The boy does not take any medications.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for that information. Since he is a 5-year-old with new-onset hypertension and no family history of cardiac disease, is there any possibility he has been taking over-the-counter medication like decongestants, or does he have any symptoms like headaches, vomiting, or vision changes?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is High blood pressure on the right upper extremity.

speaker: Doctor
text: That is a very specific and important finding; right-sided hypertension in a child strongly suggests coarctation of the aorta. Can you tell me exactly where you felt or were told the blood pressure was high, and does he have any cold hands or weak pulses in his legs? REQUEST TEST: Upper and lower extremity blood pressure comparison; REQUEST TEST: Physical examination of femoral and dorsalis pedis pulses.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Coarctation of the Aorta.

The clinical presentation of significantly higher blood pressure in the right upper extremity compared to the lower extremities, combined with weak femoral pulses and echocardiographic confirmation of aortic narrowing distal to the left subclavian artery, is diagnostic for coarctation of the aorta.
